extracted.intended_audience: courtiers, noblemen and women, and readers seeking guidance on Renaissance courtly conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on the virtues, manners, wit, and behaviours befitting an ideal Courtier and an ideal Court Lady at a Renaissance court. Covers acceptable joking, love and deceit, social graces, household duties, bodily exercises, and the balance of feminine comportment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasteful practical joking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier's practical jokes ought to be somewhat farther removed from scurrility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care must be taken not to let practical joking degenerate into knavery; tricks must not be too rude; above all pay respect and reverence to women in such jests, especially where their honour may be touched. Examples/anti-patterns: petty rogues' wiles to get money are condemnable; scurrilous or heartless pranks that leave someone wronged are improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not taunt women about chastity
rubrics_metrics.description: He who is discreet and courteous must never taunt [women] with lack of chastity, either in jest or in earnest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because in women 'free living' is treated as utter infamy and can disgrace her forever (whether the imputation is true or false), attacking women's honour by words or deeds exceeds the bounds befitting a gentleman. Even veiled or remote insinuations can be unseemly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour should rely on incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is aroused by certain things that are incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taunts about defects that are common or 'permitted' in a group (and therefore not incongruous) will not arouse true laughter; effective pleasantries should aim at incongruity rather than simply pointing out commonplace faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit must avoid scurrility and disgrace
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphor or retort, though clever, may still be scurrilous and disgraceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witty language should be apt and not obscene or degrading; being clever is not sufficient excuse for coarse or dishonouring remarks (example: a clever hunting-metaphor that equates a woman with 'heads of game' was judged scurrilous and unseemly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and truthfulness in love
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman of worth, who is in love, ought to be sincere and truthful in this as in all things; betraying even an enemy is vile, and more heinous when committed against one whom we love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim of love should be conquest of the mind rather than merely of the body; pursuing desires by treachery or trickery harms others and deprives the pursuer of true pleasure. Avoid deception that forces another's will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit enchantments, charms, and coercion in love
rubrics_metrics.description: The same I say of certain others who use enchantments in their love, charms and sometimes force, sometimes sleeping potions and such like things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods are morally condemned as improper means of securing affection or physical intimacy. They are distinguished from acceptable courtship efforts and are treated as reprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not buy love with gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts much lessen the pleasures of love; for a man may suspect that he is not loved and that his lady makes a show of loving him in order to profit by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive reliance on presents to secure affection breeds suspicion and reduces the perceived sincerity of love; genuine affection is preferable to purchased displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show reverence and discretion toward women generally
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fitting for the Courtier to show women the greatest reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men of discretion and courtesy should treat women with respect in word and deed; this general comportment underlies many specific rules about jokes, retorts, and conduct at court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared intellectual virtues (prudence, magnanimity, continence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain faculties of the mind are as necessary to woman as to man (such as prudence, magnanimity, continence, and many others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are core virtues both sexes should cultivate; they form the intellectual and moral basis of courtly behaviour and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household and managerial duties (for married women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities that befit all women such as kindness, discretion, ability to manage her husband's property and her house and children if she be married, and all those capacities requisite in a good housewife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to courtly accomplishments, a woman who is married should competently manage domestic and familial responsibilities; these practical skills are part of her virtue and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation; be naturally graceful and mannerly
rubrics_metrics.description: She ought to have gentle birth, to avoid affectation, to be naturally graceful in all her doings, to be mannerly, clever, prudent, not arrogant, not envious, not slanderous, not vain, not quarrelsome, not silly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalness and grace are prized over pretension. The Court Lady's deportment should combine intelligence and modesty; the list of vices to avoid indicates concrete anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how to win and keep favour; practise fitting accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: To know how to win and keep the favour of her mistress and of all others, to practise well and gracefully the exercises that befit women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social skill and appropriate accomplishments (conversation, entertainments, modest exercises) are essential to succeed at court; practice them gracefully and suited to rank and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty and circumspection; avoid giving rise to suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is more necessary to her than to the Courtier... she ought to be more circumspect and take greater care not to give occasion for evil being said of her, and so to act that she may not only escape a stain of guilt but even of suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because women have fewer means to defend themselves against false imputations, they must be especially careful to avoid situations or behaviours that could be misinterpreted; appearance and conduct both matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant affability and the mean between extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain pleasant affability is befitting, whereby she may be able to entertain politely every sort of man with agreeable and seemly converse, suited to the time and place, and to the rank of the person... uniting with calm and modest manners, and with that seemliness which should ever dispose all her actions, a quick vivacity of spirit whereby she may show herself alien to all indelicacy... she must preserve a certain mean (difficult and composed almost of contraries), and must barely touch certain limits but not pass them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal is balanced sociability: lively but modest, agreeable but chaste, adaptable to rank and occasion. Overstepping into coyness or forwardness are both faults; aim for the subtle mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prudishness that conceals faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus, in her wish to be thought good and pure, the Lady ought not to be so coy and seem so to abhor company and talk that are a little free, as to take her leave as soon as she finds herself therein; for it might easily be thought that she was pretending to be thus austere in order to hide something about herself which she feared others might come to know; and such prudish manners are always odious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive avoidance of convivial company or feigned austerity is interpreted as suspicious and is disfavoured; display natural modesty rather than affected prudishness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtier's service and bodily accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief profession of the Courtier... that of arms... the service of the Prince's person, and bodily exercises such as riding, handling weapons and wrestling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Courtier should be skilled in martial arts and in the physical services of court (riding, weapons, wrestling); these are proper accomplishments that lend grace and utility to his role.
